merge.title: Merge {label} into another server
merge.description: Use this when this host is one you already have — a server that was re-imaged and came back with a new machine ID, or a clone that was separated out. The reporting key moves to the server you pick, so it keeps receiving reports; this row is archived.
merge.suggestionsDescription: These servers report the same hardware serial or network card address as this one. A suggestion, not a decision — pick one only if you know that box was re-imaged.
merge.targetDescription: The server you pick keeps its own name, kind, position, owner and asset link. Everything the agent owns moves onto it with the reporting key: the reported hardware and software facts, the status, the last check-in and the agent version — and the IP too, unless that IP was set by hand. If it already reports through an agent of its own, that key is replaced: a host still checking in with it will come back as a new pending server.

confirm.title: Confirm this server
confirm.description: Add this agent-discovered host to your live topology. You can re-classify or rename it first.
confirm.trackAsAssetDescription: On by default — also create a tracked Asset (with the reported host facts) so this server can carry an owner, KB links and secrets. Turn off to keep it graph-only.
confirm.adoptExisting: This machine is already in your inventory. Confirming links it to that asset instead of creating a second one:

onboarding.title: Track servers automatically
onboarding.description: Install a lightweight agent on a Linux or Windows server and it reports its hardware & software to lazyit by itself — it can only report, nothing else.
onboarding.noPermissionHint: Ask an administrator to add a reporting agent — it needs the manage-settings permission.

add.agentDescription: Best for a server: it fills in its own hardware, software and status, and goes offline on its own when it stops checking in.
add.manualDescription: For anything that can't run an agent — a switch, a firewall, a NAS. You keep it up to date yourself.

wizard.title: Create a reporting agent
wizard.subtitle: Install a reporting agent on a Linux or Windows server in three steps.
wizard.whatIsAgent: An agent is a tiny program you run on a server. It reports the server's hardware and installed software to lazyit by itself — it can't read or change anything else.
wizard.nameHint: A name to recognise this agent later (for example the server's name).
wizard.scopeNote: This token can only report inventory (infra:report). It can't read or change anything else, and every host it reports lands in Pending review for your approval.

requirements.linux: You'll run this on a Linux server with systemd and curl, as root.
requirements.windows: You'll run this from an elevated PowerShell (right-click PowerShell → Run as administrator) on Windows 10/11 or Windows Server 2016 or newer, on x64. There's no ARM64 build, and the installer stops on any host that isn't x64. Nothing else to install: the agent is a single self-contained executable — no Node, no dependencies.

installHint.linux: Copy the command and run it on the Linux server as root. The first line hands the token over through the environment, so it never appears in the process list. The token is shown only once — capture it before closing.
installHint.windows: Copy the command and run it from an elevated PowerShell. The first line hands the token over through the environment, so it stays off the command line; the script-block form is deliberate: a plain irm | iex pipe can't pass the URL. The token is shown only once — capture it before closing.

wizard.hypervisorNote: Installing on a hypervisor host (Proxmox VE, Hyper-V, libvirt/KVM)? There's nothing extra to do: this exact same command detects the platform and inventories its guests automatically. <link>How it works</link>

advanced.noHypervisorHint: Adds {flag} to the command above: the host keeps a local veto (LAZYIT_COLLECT_HYPERVISOR=false in its config file) that wins over anything set in lazyit and survives upgrades.

wizard.unsigned: The Windows executable isn't code-signed yet, so SmartScreen will warn about it and some antivirus products may quarantine it. That's a deliberate state for internal validation, not a sign the download is wrong.

diagnostics.title: Check the host afterwards
diagnostics.hint: Read-only: it sends nothing and changes nothing. It answers whether this host can reach lazyit and whether its token is good.
diagnostics.windowsNote: Run it from an elevated PowerShell: the agent's config file can only be read by SYSTEM and Administrators, so without elevation the check reports that no URL and no token are configured. The path is written out in full because this console cannot see the folder the installer just put on PATH — a running PowerShell keeps the environment it started with, so the bare lazyit-agent test only works in one opened after the install.

wizard.waitDescription: Run the install command on your server. As soon as the agent checks in, it'll show up here — usually within a couple of minutes.
wizard.successDescription: Your server checked in. Confirm it to add it to your inventory.

bulk.title: {count, plural, one {# host can be updated} other {# hosts can be updated}}
bulk.subtitle: One command per platform, identical on every host — nothing in it is per-machine, because each host re-runs from the config it already has. Hand it to whatever already runs commands on those hosts (Ansible, a GPO startup script, Intune). Re-running the installer is safe: it re-verifies the download, keeps each host's own settings, and the host keeps its identity in lazyit.
bulk.copyAll: Or copy the whole set, annotated with which hosts each command is for:
bulk.scriptHeadline: lazyit agent update — {count, plural, one {# host} other {# hosts}} behind (instance {version})
bulk.scriptCredentialNote: No token and no URL to fill in: --upgrade re-runs each host from the config it already has. Do NOT set LAZYIT_TOKEN — it is refused alongside --upgrade.

unknownNote.body: {count, plural, one {# agent reports a version lazyit cannot compare} other {# agents report a version lazyit cannot compare}} — agents installed before version stamping report `dev`. They are never treated as behind, and each one moves into a real bucket the first time you re-run its install command. That first update is the one lazyit cannot help you with.
unknownNote.devServer: This instance reports its own version as `dev`, so no agent can be compared against it and {count, plural, one {# agent stays} other {# agents stay}} in "version unknown". Run a released build to get a real distribution.
unknownNote.help: <link>How the reporting agent stays current</link> explains what re-running the installer does and does not change.

identities.title: {count, plural, one {# agent token has never been used} other {# agent tokens have never been used}}
identities.body: A token was created for a host that never checked in — the install probably failed, or was never run. There is no node to show for it, which is why it is named here.

command.title: Update {host}
command.subtitle: This host reports agent {agentVersion}; this instance runs {serverVersion}. Run the command on the host — nothing is sent to it from here.
command.credentialNote: This command carries no token and no URL — it needs neither. `--upgrade` re-runs this host with the token, instance URL and certificate authority already in its own config, so the same line works unchanged on every host and nothing about this host is re-pointed. Do not export `LAZYIT_TOKEN` for it: it is refused alongside `--upgrade`, so a token left over in your shell can never quietly override the one this host is using.
command.tokenLost: No longer have this host's token? You don't need it — the host still has it, which is what `--upgrade` uses. Only if a host has no readable config left do you need a new one from <link>Service accounts</link>: mint a token there, then install with `--url` and `--token` as you first did. Rotating is not the same thing — it invalidates the current secret, so every other host using that service account stops reporting.
command.internalCa: Behind an internal certificate authority? `--upgrade` re-uses this host's own CA setting, but the `curl`/`irm` that downloads the script above runs before that is read — so that CA still has to be in the host's system trust store, exactly as when you first installed.
command.unknownOs: This host has not reported which system it runs, so both commands are shown. Run the one that matches the host — lazyit will not guess for you.
command.verify: Afterwards, check the host without waiting for a report:
command.rerunSafe: Re-running the installer is safe on a host that already has the agent: the download is checksum-verified, the binary is tested before anything is armed, your existing settings are merged rather than replaced, and the host keeps its identity in lazyit. On a host that is already current it does nothing.

endpoints.showHint: Laptops and desktops are kept off the map so the estate stays readable. They are still in your inventory, on the Servers list and in search — this only changes what the map draws.
endpoints.hideHint: Take laptops and desktops back off the map. Nothing is removed — they stay in your inventory, on the Servers list and in search.

That usually means the machine was recorded twice, before lazyit knew how to link an existing record. Nothing has been changed and nothing will be merged for you — open the other asset to check whether it really is the same machine, then reconcile the two yourself.

changes.emptyDescription: Nothing tracked on this node has changed yet. Only real moves are recorded — a package installed, removed or upgraded, or the OS, kernel, memory, disk, serial or container image changing. A node nobody's agent reports on never gets an entry.

bulk.confirmDescription: Each item is confirmed exactly as it would be one at a time: {hosts, plural, one {# server} other {# servers}} and {containers, plural, =0 {no containers} one {# container} other {# containers}}. You are still approving every one of them.
bulk.trackHostsLabel: Track the {count, plural, one {server} other {# servers}} as inventory assets
bulk.trackHostsDescription: On by default, as for a single confirm — a server is a thing you own, assign and warranty, so it gets an Asset carrying the reported host facts.
bulk.trackContainersLabel: Track the {count, plural, one {container} other {# containers}} as inventory assets
bulk.trackContainersDescription: Off by default. A container is replaced by the next deploy, has no serial to record, and one Docker host can add dozens — so they stay on the map without adding Assets nobody will curate. Turn it on if a container really is something you track.
bulk.kindDescription: Leave this alone unless the agent got the classification wrong for the whole selection.
bulk.discardDescription: This takes them off the map. Their history is kept and they can be restored later — the same as discarding one at a time. If the agent reports them again they will come back as new pending items.
bulk.appliedToast: {count, plural, one {# item done} other {# items done}}.

rules.title: Auto-confirm rules
rules.description: Write down a judgement once instead of repeating it for every discovered host. A rule you wrote is still your decision — you can disable or delete it at any time, and every server it confirms is recorded against your name.
rules.notRetroactive: A rule only applies to reports that arrive after you save it. Nothing already waiting in this tray will be confirmed behind you — those are still yours to review.
rules.empty: No rules yet. Every discovered host waits here until you confirm it.
rules.namePlaceholder: Production servers on the management VLAN
rules.hostnameDescription: Use * for any run of characters and ? for exactly one — srv-* matches srv-app-04. The whole name has to match, not just part of it. A pattern of nothing but wildcards isn't a condition: it has to carry at least one literal character.
rules.subnetDescription: A CIDR block, IPv4 or IPv6. A host that reported no address never matches this. 0.0.0.0/0 isn't a condition either — it's every address there is.
rules.reportedKindDescription: What the agent's report made lazyit propose for this host — not what you want it to become.
rules.chassisDescription: What the machine says it physically is — read from its firmware, not from its name. This is enough of a condition on its own, so "auto-confirm the servers, review the laptops" is a rule you can write. A host that reports no form factor never matches a rule that names one.
rules.trackAsAssetDescription: On by default for a servers-only rule, off for any rule that can also match containers — the same reasoning as confirming by hand. Turn it on if these containers really are things you track.
rules.needsCondition: A rule needs at least one condition that can rule a host out: a name pattern with something other than * and ?, a subnet narrower than 0.0.0.0/0, a reported kind, or a reported form factor. Most wildcard-only patterns match every host there is, so they would confirm everything the agent finds; ? on its own matches only one-character names, and is refused along with them to keep the rule one you can check by looking.
rules.savedToast: Rule saved. It applies from the next report onwards.
rules.deletedToast: Rule deleted. Servers it already confirmed are unchanged.
rules.author: Written by {name}
rules.authorUnknown: Author no longer in the directory
